p:
Great to see you all, and thanks for being here. And Haris, happy Eid. Hope Eid was special. Okay. So, I want to start with some questions on accessibility as the Disabilities

Committee Chair. Could you share how SBS is coordinating, or not, with the Mayor's Office for People with Disabilities to ensure that business owners with disabilities are aware of the available city resources?

Thank you for the question, Council Member. So that is a very close partnership for us, in addition to our partnership with CCHR, to make sure that business owners are aware of their responsibilities with respect to accessibility laws. And also, obviously, on the contracting side, we make sure that all of our partners have accessible sites for New Yorkers.
How are you able to assess that, or how are you evaluating that small businesses are accessible infrastructure-wise and also worker protection-wise?

So, Council Member, we make available information that the agencies make available to make sure that business owners are aware of their responsibilities under the law. We are not a regulatory or enforcement agency ourselves, so we are unable to—
[interposing] got it.
to enforce the law, but we make sure that they are aware of their responsibilities under the law.
And then, are SBS's online resources, portals, application systems compliant with web content accessibility guidelines?
Yes, they are, Council Member.
Great. And then, has SBS conducted any recent audits of its digital tools and portals for accessibility compliance, and what were the findings?
We do it regularly through the course of our work.
Meaning quarterly, annually?

Thank you, Chair Hanif. Our team works closely to make sure that any documents that we put together on the internet is accessible to all, including our social media. And so that work is built into our SOPs, and it's work that is standard across our teams.

And then for businesses— business owners with disabilities and workers with disabilities, do they come to SBS for resources or small business support? And could you share what the extent of that looks like?

Yeah, so on both fronts, we serve New Yorkers with disabilities. On the workforce side, we're proud to share, even in the Commissioner's testimony, 1,300 New Yorkers with disabilities were served through our programming. And last year when City Hall put out a number on the New Yorkers that were connected to jobs that are people with disabilities, it's the city's Workforce One system that does the lion's share of that work, making sure New Yorkers can get those opportunities to have a meaningful career here. And then on the businesses side, our work is also accessible. And we really are proud of this partnership with MOPD and CCHR to ensure every year we make sure there's webinars specifically targeted to businesses on the requirements to comply with ADA in ways that could be easier for them to understand those rules and then comply with those rules.
And then for the 1,000 businesses you just highlighted, what services were specifically provided, and do those programs have any funding cuts?
Those were— I'm sorry, those were 1,300 New Yorkers connected with jobs.
Okay.

And so that reflects a partnership with employers who we really want to get even more employers that are interested and focused on this area. We want to partner with everybody. And then on the worker side, if a New Yorker with disability approaches us, we're scanning the market, trying to connect them to the jobs that they'd be interested in. And through that work, it's 1,300 New Yorkers that were served in the last fiscal year. We're already on track, and I think we've already connected 600+ New Yorkers to jobs this fiscal year before the end of the fiscal year.
That's great. Love to hear that.
Yes.

For CC— the partnership with CCHR, my understanding is CCHR has done incredible work to reach settlements for employment facilities that are not accessible and have supported workers with disabilities to ensure that their workplace is accessible. Have— how do you all participate in that? Do you— is there funding cut out for the disability-related infrastructure work and settlement work?

We haven't had resources to support compliance and physical infrastructure upgrades. There's also state and city laws that make it harder for government to pass funding to private entities to conduct that kind of infrastructural upgrade. But it's because we know that there's this challenge in understanding and then complying with these laws, we— that's exactly the reason why CCHR and MOPD and SBS work together. Just last year, when we organized the city's largest ever small business gathering, we had 3,000+ businesses in the room. At the NYC Small Business Month Expo, a particular workshop where we had 30 business owners in attendance. It was solely focused on this issue and where New Yorkers could understand and really

speak to the leadership at CCHR, MOPD, and SBS directly to understand how these laws can impact them directly and how— ways to comply and understand that it's not impossible, that there are ways in which they can meet the need that the law set out.
Chair, could I have a– and that expo that you just talked about does that have a— does— is that funding already baked into SBS, or is that–
The funding to put together the expo?
Yeah.
Sure, yes.
Okay.
Yes.

Small BIDs in my district have benefited greatly from the small BID grant. Would SBS expand this grant to increase the impact of this work, and what resources would SBS to expand the impact? Could you speak to how else SBS is supporting small BIDs?

So SBS serves as an oversight function for small BIDs to help them get started, and grants like the small BID grant, the

applications are actually opening up soon, right, in a couple of weeks. So we look forward to dispersing those funds and assisting BIDs.
And have those— are those funds increasing or are they remaining the same?
They remain stable for this fiscal year.
Got it. We can come back to that later.
Thank you, council member. I'd like to recognize Council Member Morano has joined us and he has a question.
Thank you very much. I appreciate your testimony. Good to talk with you, Commissioner.
Likewise.

You mentioned SBS has helped connect businesses to over $120 million in financing and saved $60 million in fines. Can you break down how much of that actually went to businesses in my borough of Staten Island?
We'll have to follow up with borough-specific data, Councilmember.

We have a lot of great small businesses in our– in our borough, and you highlighted success stories in Queens. I'm wondering if you can share a comparable example of an industrial business on Staten Island that benefited from SBS in the same way.

Thank you, Councilmember. So we've got our partnership with the business improvement districts on the districts– so separate from our work with the Staten Island Chamber of Commerce, separate from our in-house outreach team, we also work closely with the BID network in Staten Island. And as we shared in our opportunity to brief you on the work that's happening on the ground in the borough, it's the partnership with the BIDs where one of them is specifically focused on industrial businesses in the West Shore working with manufacturers and other industrial businesses. You also know there's the Amazon presence there. And so there's a whole set of actors there that we're supporting through our BID work in the borough of Staten Island.

In terms of that industrial BID and the West Shore, there's a March

9th RFP that restructures the Industrial Business Zone program. I'm wondering if you can explain why SBS is moving away from a dedicated industrial service model to a consolidated one?
Sure, Council Member. So the intent of the RFP is to make the industrial business services available citywide, not just within the IBZs.
So was Staten Island's existing IBSP model, which has been in place for years, I think over a decade, evaluated as ineffective before making this change?
That's right, right. Our intent is to reach more New Yorkers. It's not anything specific to the current service delivery.
So you spoke about partnership with communities, which is great. Were Staten Island industrial stakeholders, including existing providers, consulted before this RFP was released?

So procurement rules limit the amount of contact we can have with potential applicants to the procurement, but we did contact and engage with business stakeholders leading

up to the program design before the procurement was issued.

And, obviously Staten Island's current provider has decades of relationships with the industrial community. What safeguards are in place to ensure that institutional knowledge isn't lost if a new entity is awarded the contract?

I appreciate the question, Council Member. The RFP requires that awardees either possess at least five years of demonstrated experience serving industrial businesses or partner via subcontracting with an entity that possesses that experience. So we value that experience as well and bake that into the
Does SBS have the flexibility to adjust the targets that you're focused on now based on borough-specific conditions, or is this a one-size-fits-all model?
To answer your question, Council Member, the issue of targets, that comes later after we have selected awardees, and that's part of the contract negotiation.

This contract expands expectations significantly, more outreach, more services, a satellite location, which is terrific, but it only funds three staff members. Do you believe that staffing level is sufficient for a borough like Staten Island?
So three is the floor. That's the minimum, Council Member.

Got it. Okay, thank you. Lastly on the RFP for me. The RFP was released March 9th with an April 17th deadline. That's a very tight turnaround to design a completely new service model. Why such a compressed timeline?
Yeah, so we want to make sure that there isn't a gap in services. The contracts expire June 30th, 2026, so that was the intent there.
So, and at the end of this three-year contract, how are you going to measure whether this new model actually worked better than the current IBSP structure?

So, metrics and outcomes, those are things that we'll discuss during

the contract negotiation process once we've selected the vendors.
Thanks very much.
Thank you, Council Member.
Thank you, Chair.

Thank you, Council Member. I'd like to say we've been joined by Finance Chair Council Member Lee. So, I have a couple more questions. First, as it relates to the minority and women-owned businesses. So SBS supports minority and women-owned businesses by certifying them to compete for city contracts and increasing their visibility to agencies and private partners. It also provides training, one-on-one advising, and mentorship to help these businesses navigate procurement and growth. Overall, its work focuses on expanding access to contracts capital and opportunities to promote a more equitable local economy. So SBS exceeded its target of minority and women business awards, yet actual awards have declined from 1,903 in FY23 to 1,844 in FY25. Do you know the reason for this decrease in awards?

Thank you for the question, Chair. So, as you mentioned, SBS's role is focused on the registration, the capacity building, technical assistance, and connection to funding. With respect to actual awards that occur, we would have to defer to the Office of MWBE, who sets citywide policy on MWBE and engages agencies on their MWBE contracting efforts.
Do these agencies often reach out or coordinate with SBS when they are looking for MWBE providers?

Yes, Chair. So we have our buyer services team, which supports city agencies but also private sector actors when they're interested in working with MWBE firms. And we maintain the city's Get Certified list. So it's a publicly available list where you can find the kind of business that might make sense for the need that you have in the work that you're conducting.

I've found through practice that oftentimes when different agencies put out a procurement, they'll do like a mass blast to various companies that don't even

provide the service they're looking for. Does SBS assist in any way in helping really weed out—

[interposing] yes. Yeah. So what happens, if an agency chose to work with us, they would reach out to our team, they would tell us, hey, we're looking for X, and then our team will conduct an analysis, first scanning the industry codes in the MWBE system where vendors have already identified themselves as vendors that could deliver that work. But then on top of that, they'll look at past performance, they'll look at any other information and really the description. There's a profile that our system builds in where a business can describe the kinds of work that they do. So the team, the buyer services team will look at all of that and then give the agency a curated list of vendors that could be responsive to the need that the agency has.
Do you know offhand which agencies don't use your services in that regard?

I think it's hard to tell which agency don't, but many agencies do and even private sector partners. So when we first

started engaging with the host committee for FIFA, we asked them to consider working with the city's MWBE businesses. And we— they've asked a couple questions last year, and we followed up with curated lists of MWBE businesses that could support them in their work.
Oh, you opened up another question. Do you know, have they actually engaged any of those businesses, and how many businesses are being— are we working with for the upcoming World Cup?
We haven't heard from them on if they've engaged with the city's certified MWBEs, or have received any metrics from them on that regard.
I'd encourage you to give them a nudge. What, 80 days away? What percentage of certified MWBEs are actively receiving city contracts to your knowledge?
So in fiscal year 25, the MWBEs that won contracts represent 16 percent of the certified pool. And that reflects a trend that's been steadily increasing over the last five years.
So 16% of MWBs certified through SBS are currently receiving city contracts?
That's correct, Chair.
Okay. And since you do work with private entities as well, do they often report back when they use or engage any of the MWBEs or work with them?
No.
At this time, I'll turn it over to Chair of Finance, Council Member Lee.
Good afternoon. Sorry,
Good afternoon.

My time is warped. And thank you so much. I want to say to your Chief of Staff, Haris Khan, because he's been very helpful with our office on a bunch of different issues. So you have a great Chief of Staff.
Thank you.

And just had a couple questions. So I noticed the— for example, from FY26 to 27, the headcount is largely the same. However, it

seems like there's a pretty big drop in the overall budget. So just wanted to know if you could get some clarity on that. I see there's contract services decreases. So I just wanted to get a better sense of where that's coming from and then workforce development decreases, and how is that going to potentially impact services, which hopefully it won't? If you could go into that a little bit?
Sure. So, the decrease in the budget that you're seeing reflects pass-through funding that passes through SBS to other entities.
Like CDBG block grant funding, that kind of funding or?
No. This is for
Oh, I see, within the city.
Yes, correct. You're also seeing there the council discretionary, which has not yet been added to the budget, but we will expect that to be added in the adopted budget.
Okay, so will we see that increase go back into the budget for exec?
It's adopted budget.
Adopted. Okay. And do you— is the assumption that it's going to be similar?
Yes.

Okay, and then also, is that the same reason? Because I noticed that for the contracts, the numbers of the contracts from FY26 to 27, for example, for contractual services, it's the same number, actually. There's only one contract that's different, but then the amount is pretty— the delta in the amount is $129,000 versus $58,000. So I was just wondering why that decrease is happening and which contract. And then also same thing with economic development. It went from $61.6 to $42.9 with the same number of contracts. And so just wanting to know what that difference is.

Thank you for the question, Chair. So, in the fiscal year 27 prelim plan there's a difference of three contracts overall, three contracts less, and these are all EDC contracts. The single largest drop is an EDC contract.

Okay. Because the number of contracts are the same according to the OMB sheet

here. That's why I'm wondering where the difference in funding is.

Yeah, what we're showing is that there are three less contracts overall, and the single biggest drop is an EDC contract for $31.2 million. We also have some SBS program contracts that are ending this year, but will be— they're in the procurement pipeline to be put back into the plan. So there's really no– you know, at the end of the day when analyzing this, there's no change regarding SBS contracting for our core services.

Okay, and then those will also be put back in during adopt— during the adoption process. Okay. And then, I see here for new needs it went up from FY26 to 27. So new needs in FY26 was about 2.7, and then in FY20— sorry, FY26, 2.7, and then FY27, it's about 5.3. So just wanted to know– I know that there's some things you highlighted including New York City BEST and some other increases, and just wanted to know if you could go into a little bit more of the new needs portion?

Sure. So $4 million baseline for the new needs is for NYC BEST to hire

those 30 staff lines. There's some small OTPS associated with that as well. There's about $430,000 licensing software for CRM system that we use to track service delivery. And then there are smaller grants for several bids. I think the Long Island City BID, Jamaica as well–
[interposing] Right.
In addition to a cost of living adjustment at $400K.
Okay, and that's for all of the staff currently, correct? That are line item? Okay.
Yes.

Perfect. So for– I know that you guys all submitted your savings plans last Friday and just wanted to know, because there were 92 vacancies and 300 active staff at SBS at the end of January for 23 percent vacancy rate. So just wanted to know how that's changed, maybe if you have updated numbers and how much anticipated accruals you're looking at for that.

Sure. So the number of vacancies at SBS excluding like, talent and another pass-through entities is 38 to date. And you

know, we were actively recruiting and trying to hire up those vacancies. SBS is still under the two-for-one hiring freeze, so that poses a challenge.
Okay, got it.
But the–
When is that going to be, you know, turned off, I guess, or lifted?
Hopefully soon.

Okay, got it. Okay. And then in terms of the grant loans— grants, loans, and financial assistance– and apologies if you went over this already in your testimony. How much funding is allocated for grants, loans, or financial assistance programs to small businesses for FY27?

So just last week, together with the mayor, we announced the NYC Future Fund. It's a brand new loan initiative, first in the city to provide businesses who experience seasonal revenue changes with a loan product that fits their needs and helps even out their revenue. And that's an $80 million fund.

Okay, perfect. And then how— I think, you know, obviously we're worried about the recent news that the Trump administration had put

out ending SBA loans to immigrant-owned businesses, and how do you anticipate that having an impact on the economic growth of our city?

Yeah, I think any time you– you know, over half of the businesses in New York City are immigrant-owned and operated, so any time you remove a significant financing source, that there will be an impact there. At SBS, we don't receive SBA loan funding, so we're focused on directing businesses to the loan products we do have available, such as the Future Fund, and to our Fund Finder resource where we partner them with responsible lenders to find a loan product that suits their needs.
And I'm assuming you partner with all the CDFIs.
All the CDFIs, yes.
Doing great work in the community. So– especially the immigrant community. So that's great to hear. Have you asked for additional funding from the state also during the budget process?
No, we're city funded.
Okay, so there's nothing there that the state would be able to help with in terms of economic development or MWBE programs?
No, not that we're aware of.
Okay. And then what programs have seen increased funding without proportional outcomes and improvements?

I don't think that we have programs that have gotten increased funding and have lower outcomes, but we certainly did an analysis across the board of all of our programs to kind of look to optimize and look for efficiencies and ways to serve more people and more small businesses as part of the savings plan exercise.

Okay, great. That's good to hear. And then on the flip side of that, were there examples where the funding was decreased but the outcomes remained the same because you were able to hold the line, so to speak?

I think some of that kind of ties into some of the questions that have been asked about the vacancy rate. So I

think that that's a way to look at it, and I think across the board, even though we've been subject to and challenged by the two-for-one hiring. I think by and large, our program outcomes are very, very good. And if you kind of factor out— I think the other kind of theme of some of the questioning is the PMMR indicators are hard for us because many of our indicators measure outcomes, and outcomes don't happen in the four-month PMMR period. So when you get to the end at the MMR, and like, if you look at the last MMR, you'll see pretty much across the board, we're hitting all of our goals, all of our metrics, even though we haven't been able to fully hire all of the staff that we're allocated for.
But I'm assuming that you are able to track that and predict those things along the way throughout the fiscal year, correct? Based— yeah.
Yeah, we're monitoring– we're monitoring the outputs of the programs.
Right.
The MMR and the PMMR, monitoring the outcomes. And that's why when you do the four-month look–
[interposing] Right, you're not yet seeing all of the outcomes.

Right, yep. Yeah, trust me, on the nonprofit side, I had to deal with that all the time where our contracts wouldn't get registered, but we had to sort of juggle all of that stuff around. And then for the Future Fund that you just mentioned, do you have the capacity for the new workload? How are you sort of gearing up for that?
Absolutely. We have the capacity. We're doing a lot of outreach. I think in the last week, we've received over 200 applications since the announcement.

Great to hear. And what businesses most need, from your vantage point, SBS support? And what type of research has SBS done to prioritize directing its resources? And I would just like to add in there, including, you know, outreach to a lot of the different languages spoken for the business owners. Because I know that even in my district alone, there are so many dialects and

languages spoken. So if you could speak to that as well.
